title: Prisons: Not as Fun as You'd Think
summary: Josh and Chuck explore American prisons: security levels (minimum, medium, maximum, supermax), the origins of supermax and solitary confinement, the intake process ("fish tank," diesel bus), prison jobs and pay, cells, head counts, commissary, black market and prison wine (pruno), visitation and conjugal visits, prison rape statistics, guard misconduct and discipline (shots), prison uprisings (Attica, New Mexico State Pen), reentry, education, recidivism, incarceration costs, and prison movies. Ends with a note that there is no listener mail this episode.

segments.title: Opening banter and prison statistics
segments.summary: Hosts open with a correction on crack sentencing disparity and discuss public views of prisoners, then cite statistics on the number of Americans in prison and Georgia's high incarceration rate.

segments.title: Security levels of US prisons
segments.summary: Overview of minimum, medium, and maximum security prisons, with descriptions of dorm-style medium security housing and the typical inmates at each level.

segments.title: Supermax prisons and solitary confinement
segments.summary: The 1993 Marion, Illinois lockdown led to the supermax model. The hosts describe solitary confinement's origins in 1830 Pennsylvania, its psychological effects, the spread of supermax prisons in the 1990s, and suicides and self-harm in these facilities. ADX Florence is the only federal supermax.

segments.title: Getting to prison and intake
segments.summary: Ways of getting to prison, including taxi, drop-off, and the prison bus nicknamed the diesel tour. New inmates, called fish, are processed in the fish tank and segregated for about thirty days.

segments.title: Prison jobs, cells, and daily structure
segments.summary: Prison jobs pay very little; one ex-inmate's account describes a dorm janitor paid forty cents a day. Cells are typically about eight by six feet, often overcrowded with added bunks. Guards perform regular head counts and night counts.

segments.title: Commissary, black market, and pruno
segments.summary: Inmates buy approved items from the commissary using an account linked to an ID card. A black market trades cigarettes and favors. Pruno, homemade prison wine, is described.

segments.title: Prison visitation and conjugal visits
segments.summary: Visitation is limited by an assigned number of visits and an approved list, with searches on entry. Conjugal visits began in Mississippi in 1918 and are now in a handful of states under the Extended Family Program, limited to married spouses, with gay domestic partners eligible in some places.

segments.title: Prison sexual abuse and guard misconduct
segments.summary: Statistics on prison rape vary by source; a 2007 Bureau of Justice figure is cited, along with the Prison Rape Elimination Act and zero tolerance policies. Guards are described as capable of misconduct, and disciplinary measures include shots and loss of good time.

segments.title: Prison uprisings: Attica and New Mexico
segments.summary: The hosts describe the Attica uprising in New York in 1971, where guards and prisoners died when the state stormed the prison, and the New Mexico State Penitentiary riot near Santa Fe, where inmates were killed.

segments.title: Reform, education, recidivism, and cost
segments.summary: Discussion of prison reform, education programs such as GED courses, recidivism rates (about 67 percent in 1994, lower since), and the roughly fifty-one billion dollars spent on incarceration.

segments.title: Prison movies and sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts list favorite prison films, including Shawshank Redemption, Escape from Alcatraz, and Animal Factory, then note there is no listener mail this week and invite listeners to write in.
